questions.q: How does a monitoring baseline (this lesson) differ from the performance baseline from Lesson 3?
options: A monitoring baseline is a recurring, scheduled capture that builds a historical record over time, rather than a single point-in-time snapshot
They are exactly the same thing with different names
A monitoring baseline only applies to Azure SQL Database
A monitoring baseline replaces the need to ever look at wait statistics
questions.explain: Lesson 3's baseline is one snapshot for one project; a monitoring baseline captures metrics on a schedule so you build a real historical pattern to compare against.

questions.q: Why must a metric like sys.dm_os_wait_stats be diffed between two snapshots rather than read as a single raw value?
options: Because wait stats are cumulative since the last restart (or manual clear), so the raw total doesn't tell you what happened in any specific window of time
Because sys.dm_os_wait_stats resets itself every 15 minutes automatically
Because wait stats are not a real DMV
Because raw values are always reported in the wrong unit
questions.explain: Wait stats accumulate since the last restart or manual clear; only the delta between two snapshots reflects what happened during that specific interval.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what's a practical capture interval for a recurring monitoring snapshot?
options: Something like every 15 minutes, on a schedule, via a SQL Server Agent job
Once per year, during the annual server review
Only during a live outage
Every time a user complains about slowness
questions.explain: The lesson suggests a fixed schedule such as every 15 minutes so the history table builds a real pattern across hours, days, and workload cycles.

questions.q: Which of these DMVs does the lesson call out as a useful source for a recurring monitoring snapshot?
options: sys.dm_os_performance_counters, for metrics like Page Life Expectancy and Batch Requests/sec
sys.databases, for database creation dates
sys.objects, for a list of table names
sys.dm_exec_connections, for a list of open connections only
questions.explain: The lesson names sys.dm_os_wait_stats, sys.dm_os_performance_counters, and sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats as the DMVs worth capturing on a recurring schedule.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend storing snapshots in a permanent table rather than just querying the DMVs live whenever you want to check?
options: A live DMV query only shows the current cumulative state — without stored history, you have no way to compare "now" against what's actually normal for that time of day or week
DMVs are deleted every time SQL Server restarts, so querying them live is impossible
Permanent tables run faster than DMV queries
Storing history is required by SQL Server licensing
questions.explain: Without a stored historical record, there's nothing to compare a live reading against besides a guess — the whole point of the history table is building that real comparison baseline.
